question: What are HTTP status code ranges and what does each range mean?
title: HTTP Status Code Ranges
direct_answer: HTTP status codes are grouped into five ranges: 1xx (informational), 2xx (success), 3xx (redirection), 4xx (client errors), and 5xx (server errors). In REST APIs, you'll primarily use 2xx to indicate successful operations and 4xx/5xx to communicate different types of failures to the client.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand HTTP semantics and can choose appropriate status codes for different API scenarios in a REST API context
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning 200 OK for all responses and embedding error information in the JSON body instead of using proper status codes to communicate the actual outcome
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention specific codes like 201 for resource creation, 204 for successful deletes without response body, 409 for conflicts, and 422 for validation failures with proper Location headers

sections.title: HTTP Status Code Ranges Explained
sections.content:
HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers that the server sends to tell the client what happened with their request. Think of them like traffic signals: **1xx codes** are informational (green light, keep going), **2xx codes** mean success (you made it), **3xx codes** handle redirection (go somewhere else), **4xx codes** indicate client errors (you did something wrong), and **5xx codes** signal server errors (we messed up).

In a Spring Boot REST API serving a mobile client, you'll mainly use **2xx** to confirm successful operations like fetching user data or updating an order, **4xx** when the client sends invalid data or lacks permissions, and **5xx** when your backend encounters database failures or unexpected exceptions. The client uses these codes to decide what to show the user: a success message, a validation error, or a retry prompt.

sections.title: Returning Different Status Codes in Spring Boot
When to Use Each Range
sections.content:
Use **2xx codes** when the operation succeeds: 200 for GET requests that return data, 201 when POST creates a new resource, 204 when DELETE succeeds but returns nothing.

Use **4xx codes** when the client makes a mistake: 400 for malformed JSON, 401 when authentication fails, 403 when the user lacks permission, 404 when the resource doesn't exist, 422 for validation errors.

Use **5xx codes** when your server encounters problems: 500 for unexpected exceptions, 503 when the database is down or the service is overloaded. In a mobile app scenario, 4xx tells the app to show the user an error message, while 5xx tells the app to retry the request later.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Always returning 200**: Many freshers return 200 OK for every response and put error details in the JSON body like {"success":false,"error":"User not found"}. This breaks HTTP semantics and makes it harder for HTTP clients, caching layers, and monitoring tools to understand what happened.
- **Confusing 4xx and 5xx**: Using 500 Internal Server Error for validation failures. If the client sent bad data, that's a 4xx error (their fault), not a 5xx error (your fault).
- **Missing Location headers**: Returning 201 Created without a Location header pointing to the new resource URI, which violates REST conventions and makes it harder for clients to fetch the created resource.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **1xx Informational**: Rarely used in REST APIs, indicates request received and processing continues
**2xx Success**: Operation completed successfully — 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content are most common
**3xx Redirection**: Resource moved, client should request different URI — rare in JSON APIs
**4xx Client Error**: Problem with the request — invalid data, missing authentication, forbidden access
**5xx Server Error**: Backend failure — database down, uncaught exception, service unavailable
**ResponseEntity in Spring**: Use ResponseEntity.ok(), ResponseEntity.created(), ResponseEntity.notFound() to set status codes cleanly
**HTTP semantics**: Proper status codes enable HTTP caching, logging, monitoring, and standard client error handling

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers grouped into five ranges that tell the client what happened with their request. The ranges are 1xx for informational responses, 2xx for success, 3xx for redirection, 4xx for client errors, and 5xx for server errors. In a REST API, you use these to communicate the outcome of operations. For example, when a mobile app creates a new order, you'd return 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource. If the app tries to fetch an order that doesn't exist, you return 404 Not Found. If the user isn't logged in, you return 401 Unauthorized. If your database goes down, you return 503 Service Unavailable. The key is that 4xx means the client did something wrong and should fix their request, while 5xx means your server had a problem and the client might retry. A common mistake freshers make is returning 200 OK for everything and embedding error details in the JSON body, which breaks HTTP semantics. In Spring Boot, you use ResponseEntity to control the status code, like ResponseEntity.created() for 201 or ResponseEntity.notFound() for 404. This helps clients, monitoring tools, and caching layers understand what happened without parsing the response body.

question: What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
title: 401 vs 403 Status Codes
direct_answer: 401 Unauthorized means authentication failed or credentials weren't provided — the user isn't logged in. 403 Forbidden means authentication succeeded but the authenticated user lacks permission to access the resource — they're logged in but authorization failed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the distinction between authentication (verifying identity) and authorization (verifying permissions) and can map them to the correct HTTP status codes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 403 when credentials are missing, or conflating authentication failures with permission denials, or using 401 when a logged-in user tries to access a forbidden resource
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that 401 should include a WWW-Authenticate header per HTTP spec, explain how Spring Security automatically maps these, and give a concrete example like admin-only endpoints

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization Errors
sections.content:
The difference between **401 Unauthorized** and **403 Forbidden** boils down to authentication versus authorization. **401** means "Who are you?" — the server doesn't know who's making the request because credentials weren't provided or were invalid. **403** means "I know who you are, but you can't do that" — the server authenticated the user successfully but they lack permission to access the resource. Think of 401 like being stopped at the door of a club because you don't have an ID, while 403 is like having an ID that proves you're 18 but the VIP section is for members only.

In a Spring Boot API, 401 typically happens when a JWT token is missing or expired, while 403 happens when a regular user tries to access an admin-only endpoint.

Prompt for login or refresh token

sections.title: When to Return Each Status Code
sections.content: Return **401 Unauthorized** when the request doesn't include valid authentication credentials: missing Authorization header, expired JWT token, invalid API key, wrong username or password. The client should respond by prompting the user to log in or refresh their authentication token. Return **403 Forbidden** when authentication succeeded but the user doesn't have permission: a regular user trying to delete another user's order, a free-tier user accessing premium features, or an employee accessing admin-only reports. The client should show an access denied message and not retry with the same credentials. In Spring Security, if you configure role-based access with at-PreAuthorize and a user with role USER tries to access a method requiring ADMIN, Spring returns 403 automatically.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using 403 for missing authentication**: Freshers often return 403 when no token is provided, but the correct code is 401 because the server doesn't know who the user is. 403 implies the server knows the user but denies access.
- **Using 401 for permission denials**: Returning 401 when a logged-in user lacks permissions. If the user is authenticated but unauthorized, that's 403.
- **Missing WWW-Authenticate header**: The HTTP spec requires 401 responses to include a WWW-Authenticate header indicating the authentication scheme, like WWW-Authenticate: Bearer. Spring Security handles this automatically, but custom auth logic often forgets it.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points

**403 Forbidden**: Authorization failed — user identity known but lacks permission
**WWW-Authenticate header**: 401 responses should include this header per HTTP spec, indicating auth scheme like Bearer or Basic
**Spring Security mapping**: Spring automatically returns 401 for auth failures and 403 for access denied based on security config
**Client behavior**: 401 triggers login prompts or token refresh, 403 shows access denied with no retry
**Common scenario**: 401 for expired JWT tokens, 403 for role-based access control failures
**At-PreAuthorize annotation**: Throws AccessDeniedException which Spring Security maps to 403

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference is about authentication versus authorization. 401 Unauthorized means authentication failed — the server doesn't know who you are because you didn't provide credentials or they were invalid. It's like trying to enter a building without showing your ID. The client should prompt the user to log in or refresh their token. 403 Forbidden means authentication succeeded but authorization failed — the server knows who you are but you don't have permission to access that resource. It's like showing your employee badge but trying to enter the executive suite when you're not an executive. The client should show an access denied message. In Spring Security, 401 happens when a JWT token is missing or expired, while 403 happens when you use at-PreAuthorize to restrict an endpoint to admins and a regular user tries to access it. A common mistake is returning 403 when no token is provided. That's wrong because 403 implies the server knows who you are but denies access. If there's no token, the server doesn't know who you are, so it should return 401. Also, 401 responses should include a WWW-Authenticate header per the HTTP spec, though Spring Security handles that automatically.

question: When do you return 200 OK vs 201 Created vs 204 No Content?
title: 200 vs 201 vs 204 Status Codes
direct_answer: Return 200 OK for successful GET, PUT, or PATCH requests that include a response body. Return 201 Created after a POST that creates a resource, and include a Location header pointing to the new resource. Return 204 No Content for successful DELETE operations or updates that don't return data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand RESTful conventions and can design APIs that follow HTTP semantics properly, especially for different CRUD operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning 200 OK for all successful operations, especially POST creates, instead of using the more precise 201 with Location header, or returning data with 204
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that 201 should include a Location header with the new resource URI like /api/orders/123, mention using ResponseEntity.created() in Spring Boot, and discuss when PUT returns 200 vs 204

sections.title: Choosing the Right Success Status Code
sections.content: While all three codes indicate success, they convey different semantics about what happened. **200 OK** is the general success code when you're returning data in the response body — typical for GET requests fetching data or PUT/PATCH updates that return the updated resource. **201 Created** signals that a new resource was created, almost always used for POST requests, and should include a **Location header** pointing to the new resource's URI so the client knows where to find it. **204 No Content** means the operation succeeded but there's no response body to send — common for DELETE operations or PUT updates where you don't need to return the updated resource to save bandwidth. The choice communicates intent: 200 says "here's your data," 201 says "I made something new," and 204 says "done, nothing to show you."

sections.title: 200 vs 201 vs 204 Status Codes at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|200 OK|~General success with response body — use for GET, PUT, PATCH when returning data
blue|201 Created|~Resource creation success — use for POST, must include Location header pointing to new resou...
emerald|204 No Content|~Success with no response body — use for DELETE or PUT when client doesn't need returned data
violet|Location header|~201 responses should include Location: /api/resource/id to tell client where to find the new...
rose|ResponseEntity.created()|~Spring Boot method that sets 201 status and Location header in one call
cyan|POST vs PUT|~POST creates new resources (201), PUT updates existing resources (200 or 204)

sections.title: Step 1: Does the Operation Create a New Resource?
sections.content: If you're handling a POST request that creates a new resource like a user, order, or blog post, return **201 Created**. Include a **Location header** with the URI of the new resource, such as Location: /api/orders/123. In Spring Boot, use ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/api/orders/" + order.id())).body(order). If you're creating multiple resources in one request, 201 is still appropriate, but the Location header might point to a collection or parent resource. Never return 200 for POST creates — 201 explicitly signals resource creation and helps clients distinguish between creates and other operations.

sections.title: Step 2: Does the Response Include a Body?
sections.content: If the operation succeeds and you're sending data back — like fetching a user profile, updating an order and returning the updated order, or searching for products — return **200 OK**. This is the default success code when you have content to show. If the operation succeeds but you're not sending any data back — like deleting a resource or updating a resource where the client already has the data — return **204 No Content**. The key difference is whether there's a response body. For example, DELETE /api/orders/123 returns 204 because there's nothing to return after deletion. PUT /api/orders/123 might return 200 with the updated order, or 204 if the client doesn't need the updated data.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using 200 for POST creates**: The biggest mistake is returning 200 OK for POST requests that create resources. Always use 201 with a Location header.
- **Missing Location header with 201**: Returning 201 without a Location header. The HTTP spec says 201 should include this header so clients can fetch the new resource.
- **Sending body with 204**: Returning 204 No Content but including a JSON body in the response. 204 means no content, so the client ignores the body. If you have data to return, use 200.
- **Using 201 for updates**: Using 201 Created for PUT or PATCH operations. 201 is for creation only — updates should return 200 or 204.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **200 OK**: General success with response body — use for GET, PUT, PATCH when returning data
**201 Created**: Resource creation success — use for POST, must include Location header pointing to new resource URI
**204 No Content**: Success with no response body — use for DELETE or PUT when client doesn't need returned data
**Location header**: 201 responses should include Location: /api/resource/id to tell client where to find the new resource
**ResponseEntity.created()**: Spring Boot method that sets 201 status and Location header in one call
**POST vs PUT**: POST creates new resources (201), PUT updates existing resources (200 or 204)
**Bandwidth consideration**: Use 204 for updates when response body would be large and client doesn't need it

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The choice depends on the operation and whether you're returning data. Use 200 OK for successful operations that return a response body, like GET requests fetching a user or PUT requests that return the updated resource. Use 201 Created specifically for POST requests that create a new resource, and you must include a Location header pointing to the new resource URI, like Location: /api/orders/123. Use 204 No Content for successful operations that don't return data, like DELETE requests or PUT updates where the client already knows the result. In Spring Boot, you'd use ResponseEntity.ok() for 200, ResponseEntity.created() for 201 with the URI, and ResponseEntity.noContent() for 204. A common mistake is returning 200 for POST creates instead of 201. The difference matters because 201 explicitly signals resource creation and the Location header tells the client where to find it. Another mistake is sending a response body with 204 — the whole point of 204 is that there's no content, so if you have data to return, use 200 instead. For example, DELETE /api/orders/123 should return 204, but POST /api/orders should return 201 with the new order in the body and its URI in the Location header.

question: When do you use 400 Bad Request vs 404 Not Found vs 409 Conflict vs 422 Unprocessable Entity?
title: 4xx Status Code Distinctions
direct_answer: 400 Bad Request is for malformed request syntax (invalid JSON, wrong data types). 404 Not Found means the resource doesn't exist at that URI. 409 Conflict indicates a state conflict like duplicate entries or constraint violations. 422 Unprocessable Entity is for syntactically valid but semantically invalid requests, typically validation failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand precise error semantics and can design error responses that help clients distinguish between different failure types for better error handling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 400 as a catch-all for any client error, or confusing 409 and 422 for validation failures, or returning 404 when a resource exists but violates business rules
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring Boot's at-Valid returns 400 by default but 422 is semantically more correct for validation, explain when to use each code in practice with concrete examples, and discuss RFC 9457 ProblemDetail

sections.title: Distinguishing Client Error Types
sections.content: These four codes all signal client errors but address different failure modes. **400 Bad Request** means the request is malformed — the server can't parse it because of syntax errors like invalid JSON, missing required headers, or wrong data types. **404 Not Found** is straightforward: the resource at that URI doesn't exist, like GET /api/orders/999 when order 999 isn't in the database. **409 Conflict** indicates a state conflict where the operation is valid but can't proceed due to the current state, like trying to create a user with an email that already exists. **422 Unprocessable Entity** means the request is syntactically valid but semantically invalid — the JSON parses correctly but the data violates business rules, like an order with a negative price or a future birthdate. Choosing the right code helps the client understand whether to fix syntax, check if the resource exists, handle conflicts, or correct validation errors.

sections.title: 4xx Status Code Distinctions at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|400 Bad Request|~Malformed syntax — invalid JSON, wrong data types, missing required headers
blue|404 Not Found|~Resource doesn't exist at that URI — use for GET/PUT/DELETE on non-existent IDs
emerald|409 Conflict|~Valid request but state conflict — duplicate entries, constraint violations, business state...
violet|422 Unprocessable Entity|~Syntactically valid but semantically invalid — validation failures, business rule violations
rose|Spring Boot defaults|~at-Valid returns 400, but 422 is more precise for validation errors
cyan|Decision order|~Check parsing (400), then existence (404), then conflicts (409), then validation (422)

sections.title: Step 1: Can the Server Parse the Request?
sections.content: First check if the request is syntactically valid. If the JSON is malformed, a required header is missing, or a field has the wrong data type (sending a string where an integer is expected), return **400 Bad Request**. This is a parsing failure — the server can't even understand the request. Spring Boot automatically returns 400 for these cases through HttpMessageNotReadableException. Examples: {"price": "not-a-number"} when price should be a BigDecimal, missing Content-Type: application/json header, or unbalanced braces in JSON. The client needs to fix the request structure before retrying.

sections.title: Step 2: Does the Resource Exist?
sections.content: If the request parses correctly, check if the resource exists. For operations on specific resources like GET /api/orders/123, PUT /api/orders/123, or DELETE /api/orders/123, return **404 Not Found** if the resource doesn't exist in your database. Don't use 404 for validation failures on data within the request body — that's 422. Only use 404 when the URI itself points to a non-existent resource. In Spring, when Optional.empty() comes back from a repository findById call, return ResponseEntity.notFound().build(). The client should check if they have the right ID.

sections.title: Step 3: Is There a State Conflict?
sections.content: If the resource exists and the request is valid, check for state conflicts. Return **409 Conflict** when the operation would violate data integrity or business state constraints. Common cases: creating a user with an email that already exists (unique constraint), trying to cancel an order that's already shipped, double-booking a time slot, or decrementing inventory below zero. 409 signals that the operation is valid but can't proceed right now due to the current state — the client might need to refresh their data or take a different action. Use 409 when the conflict is about resource state, not data validity.

sections.title: Step 4: Does the Data Violate Business Rules?
sections.content: If the request parses correctly, the resource exists (if applicable), and there's no state conflict, but the data itself is invalid, return **422 Unprocessable Entity**. This is for semantic validation failures: empty required fields, invalid email formats, negative prices, quantities exceeding limits, or dates in the wrong range. Spring's at-Valid annotation throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which by default returns 400, but semantically 422 is more correct because the request is syntactically valid. Use 422 for field-level validation errors where the client needs to correct the data and resubmit.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using 400 for everything**: The most common mistake is returning 400 Bad Request for all client errors — validation failures, missing resources, conflicts. This makes it hard for clients to handle errors appropriately.
- **Confusing 409 and 422**: Using 409 for validation errors like invalid email format. 409 is for state conflicts (resource exists, but operation can't proceed), while 422 is for data validation (data format or rules violated).
- **Using 404 for validation**: Returning 404 when a user submits invalid data, like a negative price. 404 means the URI resource doesn't exist, not that the data is invalid.
- **Not customizing at-Valid responses**: Spring's at-Valid returns 400 by default, but 422 is semantically more accurate for validation failures. Many freshers don't customize this.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **400 Bad Request**: Malformed syntax — invalid JSON, wrong data types, missing required headers
**404 Not Found**: Resource doesn't exist at that URI — use for GET/PUT/DELETE on non-existent IDs
**409 Conflict**: Valid request but state conflict — duplicate entries, constraint violations, business state prevents operation
**422 Unprocessable Entity**: Syntactically valid but semantically invalid — validation failures, business rule violations
**Spring Boot defaults**: at-Valid returns 400, but 422 is more precise for validation errors
**Decision order**: Check parsing (400), then existence (404), then conflicts (409), then validation (422)
**Client actions**: 400 means fix syntax, 404 means check ID, 409 means refresh state, 422 means fix data

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These four status codes cover different types of client errors, and picking the right one helps the client handle failures correctly. 400 Bad Request is for malformed requests — when the JSON doesn't parse, a data type is wrong, or required headers are missing. It's a syntax error. 404 Not Found means the resource at that URI doesn't exist, like when you try to fetch order 999 but it's not in the database. 409 Conflict indicates a state conflict where the operation is valid but can't proceed because of the current state, like trying to create a user with an email that already exists or canceling an order that's already shipped. 422 Unprocessable Entity is for validation failures — the request is syntactically correct but the data violates business rules, like a negative price or an invalid email format. A common mistake freshers make is using 400 for everything, which makes it hard for clients to distinguish between syntax errors and validation failures. Another mistake is confusing 409 and 422 — use 409 for state conflicts and 422 for data validation. In Spring Boot, at-Valid returns 400 by default, but you can customize it to return 422, which is semantically more accurate. The decision order is: first check if the request parses (400), then check if the resource exists (404), then check for state conflicts (409), and finally validate the data (422).

values: Fix the request format and resend
Resolve the conflict (use a different email, reload the resource)
Fix the input values and resend

beats.text: Think of it this way: 400 is a syntax problem, 422 is a value problem, 409 is a state problem, 404 is a missing resource. In Spring Boot, @Valid throws MethodArgumentNotValidException which maps to 400 by default — many teams override this to 422 for validation failures.

items: You're returning 400 for validation failures — 422 is more semantically correct; the JSON parsed fine, the values are wrong
You're returning 400 for a duplicate email conflict — that's 409; the request was valid, the state is the problem

speakable_v2.cap: 400 = malformed request. 404 = resource missing. 409 = state conflict. 422 = valid request, invalid values. Each tells the client a different thing to do next.

sections.title: Centralized Error Handling in Spring Boot
sections.content:
In production REST APIs, you need consistent error responses across all endpoints so clients can parse errors reliably. Spring Boot provides **at-ControllerAdvice** to handle exceptions globally instead of writing try-catch blocks in every controller. You create a class annotated with at-ControllerAdvice and add **at-ExceptionHandler** methods that catch specific exceptions and return structured responses. Spring Boot 3 introduced **ProblemDetail** (based on RFC 9457), a standard JSON format for errors with fields like **type** (error category URI), **title** (short error description), **status** (HTTP code), **detail** (specific error message), and **instance** (request URI).

This gives you a consistent error structure that clients can parse, logs errors for debugging, and keeps sensitive information like stack traces out of responses.

Without this, different endpoints might return different error formats, making client-side error handling fragile.

sections.title: Implementing Global Error Handler with ProblemDetail
When to Use Global Error Handling
sections.content:
Use **at-ControllerAdvice** in every Spring Boot REST API to ensure consistent error responses. It's especially critical when multiple teams or mobile clients consume your API and need predictable error formats.

Use **ProblemDetail** when you want to follow RFC 9457 standards, which many HTTP clients and API gateways understand. Add custom **at-ExceptionHandler** methods for domain-specific exceptions like EntityNotFoundException, DuplicateResourceException, or InsufficientInventoryException, mapping each to the appropriate HTTP status code. Always include a catch-all Exception handler that returns 500 and logs the full error server-side but doesn't expose internal details to clients. This prevents sensitive information leaks and unhandled exceptions from returning Spring's default Whitelabel Error Page with stack traces.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No global error handler**: Letting exceptions bubble up unhandled, resulting in Spring's default error page or inconsistent error formats across endpoints. Every REST API needs at-ControllerAdvice.
- **Leaking stack traces**: Returning full stack traces in production responses. Stack traces expose internal implementation details and file paths. Log them server-side but return generic messages to clients.
- **Using 200 with error bodies**: Returning 200 OK with {"success":false,"error":"..."} in the body instead of proper HTTP status codes. Use at-ControllerAdvice to map exceptions to correct status codes.
- **Inconsistent error formats**: Some endpoints return {"error":"message"}, others return {"message":"error"}, and some return plain strings. ProblemDetail solves this by standardizing the structure.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **At-ControllerAdvice**: Global exception handler annotation that applies to all controllers in the application
**At-ExceptionHandler**: Method-level annotation that catches specific exception types and returns custom responses
**ProblemDetail**: Spring Boot 3 class implementing RFC 9457 with standard fields like type, title, status, detail, instance
**ResponseEntity**: Return ResponseEntity with appropriate HTTP status and ProblemDetail body
**Logging**: Always log full exception details server-side for debugging but don't expose them in API responses
**Validation errors**: Handle MethodArgumentNotValidException to return 422 with field-level error details
**Security**: Never return stack traces, database errors, or internal paths in production responses

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To implement consistent error responses in Spring Boot, you use at-ControllerAdvice with at-ExceptionHandler methods. You create a class annotated with at-ControllerAdvice and add methods annotated with at-ExceptionHandler that catch specific exception types and return structured error responses. Spring Boot 3 introduced ProblemDetail, which implements RFC 9457 and provides a standard JSON format for errors with fields like type, title, status, detail, and instance. For example, you'd handle EntityNotFoundException by returning a ProblemDetail with 404 Not Found status. You'd handle MethodArgumentNotValidException from at-Valid by extracting field errors and returning 422 Unprocessable Entity with the validation details. You always include a catch-all Exception handler that logs the full error server-side but returns a generic 500 Internal Server Error message to the client without exposing stack traces. A common mistake freshers make is letting exceptions bubble up unhandled, which results in Spring's default Whitelabel Error Page or inconsistent error formats. Another mistake is returning stack traces in production, which leaks internal implementation details. You should log the full error for debugging but only return safe, user-friendly messages to clients. This approach ensures every endpoint returns errors in the same format, making it easier for mobile apps or frontend clients to parse and display errors consistently.

speakable_v2.hook: Without a global exception handler, Spring Boot returns HTML error pages or inconsistent JSON — @ControllerAdvice is how you take control.

beats.text: @ControllerAdvice is a Spring class that acts as a global interceptor for exceptions thrown by any controller. You write @ExceptionHandler methods inside it that catch specific exception types and return consistent, structured error responses.

Without it, every controller would need its own try-catch, and Spring would fall back to its Whitelabel Error Page (HTML) or expose a default JSON error map that leaks implementation details. @ControllerAdvice gives you a single place to handle all errors consistently.

items: @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class): returns 404 with a clean error body
@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class): returns 400 or 422 with field-level validation errors
@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class): catch-all that returns 500 — never expose stack traces in production
Spring Boot 3 ProblemDetail (RFC 9457): built-in standard error format with type, title, status, detail, and instance fields

beats.text: Task app: when GET /tasks/999 throws TaskNotFoundException, the @ExceptionHandler maps it to 404 with {status: 404, message: Task not found, timestamp: 2026-06-02T10:00:00}. When POST /tasks with an invalid body triggers @Valid failure, the @ExceptionHandler for MethodArgumentNotValidException collects field errors and returns 422 with {errors: [{field: title, message: must not be blank}]}. In Spring Boot 3, you can extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler and return ProblemDetail objects for RFC-compliant error responses. production trap: the catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) must log the stack trace server-side but must never include it in the response body — stack traces reveal internal structure to attackers.

items: Including stack traces in error responses — log them, don't send them; they reveal internal details to attackers
Not having a catch-all handler — without one, unhandled exceptions return Spring's Whitelabel page or inconsistent format

speakable_v2.cap: @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler = one place for all error handling. Map exceptions to status codes, return a consistent body, never expose stack traces.
